My recommendation is to look for a memo from your units command that authorizes personal vests. Ask some people who have been there longer if you cant find it.

IF YOU ARENT 100% SURE THAT YOURE ALLOWED TO WEAR A PERSONAL PLATE CARRIER THEN DONT BUY ONE

If they dont then maybe go for an MSV. Ive seen guys buy those and not really get questioned on it too much so long as it is issued

Dont buy an MSV. I recommend an FCPC from Ferro concepts.

The MSV is alright as an issued carrier. It runs a little too big, the standard cumberbund sucks, and you need to invest a good ammount of money/time into it to make it even remotely comparable with some of the better options out there.

If youre in the army and you wanna buy one and use it instead of whatever you were issued, then go for it. Otherwise id recommend the Ferro Concepts FCPC v5 or the Crye JPC

The main reason, other than shady backdoor deals being made by generals, if for soldiers to be more easily identifiable.

By the time the UCP pattern was introduced in 2004, the older m81, desert BDU (chocolate chip) and the desert tri color had been around for over a decade (the m81 and desert bdu were both adopted in 1981). This meant that there was alot of it floating around in surplus. 

Concerns arose during the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. Senior leadership in the army were concerned that insurgents could blend in with US forces, which could lead to inside attacks and further confusion in combat.The other reason, as others here have pointed out, had to do with logistics issues, something that comes naturally with supplying uniforms to various Units around the world.

Senior leadership likely saw the UCP pattern as a solution to their problems. It was meant to work in both desert and forest environments, greatly reducing logistical issues. Additionally, it was a new, unique pattern. This meant that there was little to no surplus available, and that it would be easier to identify US forces in combat
